title: Derive tank and heater models from conservation laws
equipment: Constant-area buffer tank and electrically heated vessel
physicalPurpose: Explain integrating and self-regulating responses by deriving mass-volume and energy balances with physical units.
objective: Derive an executable buffer tank and heated vessel model from conservation laws, predict their responses with units, and decide whether the simulator agrees.

simplifications: The tank has constant area, constant density, no overflow, and independently prescribed inlet and outlet flows.
The vessel is perfectly mixed with constant thermal capacitance and linear heat loss in the declared operating region.
Sensor dynamics, evaporation, temperature-dependent properties, nonlinear gravity outflow, and unmeasured disturbances are absent.

baseline.limitation: Integrating and self-regulating labels describe curve shapes but do not explain their physical causes or parameter dependence.

change.decision: Accept each model only when its unit-consistent first-principles prediction matches the independent simulator response within declared tolerances.

abortPredicates: Any command or process value is nonfinite
The monitored model parameters or sample interval differ from the prediction
safety.restorationMode: Return tank net flow and heater command to zero, then restore both declared initial states
simulationOnlyRestrictions: This combined workshop is simulation-only. Physical flow and heater tests require separate reviewed topology, limits, operating procedures, and immediate approval.

video.viewerOutcome: Derive, predict, and validate an integrating tank and self-regulating heater from conservation laws.

learning.context: A constant-area buffer tank stores liquid and a well-mixed electrically heated vessel stores thermal energy.
learning.reason: Response-class labels from Lesson 32 do not explain the physical causes or parameter dependence of integration and self-regulation.
theory: Accumulation equals total rate entering minus total rate leaving; the stored quantity becomes a state needed to predict future behavior.
Tank level follows a volume balance, while vessel temperature follows an energy balance between heating power and temperature-dependent heat loss.
Equilibrium means zero accumulation; unit consistency and declared assumptions are prerequisites for a meaningful model.
learning.workedPrediction: The tank predicts 0.4 cm/s and 58 cm at 20 s; equal flows predict zero slope. The heater predicts 40 kW, 24 degC equilibrium, 5 s time constant, and 22.53 degC at 6 s.
practicalPreparation: Verify plant identities, units, initial states, parameters, quality, 100 ms sampling, limits, aborts, and Simulation evidence class.
Write every numerical prediction and its assumptions before starting the run.
learning.baseline: Use Lesson 32 response labels without a causal physical model and identify what they cannot predict.
learning.change: Derive both balances, run the declared unequal-flow and heater case, restore the tank, then run the equal-flow equilibrium case.
learning.comparison: Compare measured late slope, 20-second level, equal-flow drift, six-second heater temperature, final equilibrium, and late slope against declared predictions and windows.
learning.validation: Require 0.4 cm/s tank slope, 58 cm at 20 s, negligible equal-flow drift, 22.53 degC at 6 s, and qualified convergence toward 24 degC.
learning.explanation: Net flow continuously changes stored liquid, while increasing heat loss balances fixed heater power and creates a finite thermal equilibrium.
learning.transfer: Lesson 34 replaces prescribed outlet flow with nonlinear gravity outflow and derives a local linear model around an operating point.
